fixes.explanation: Job asks, “How long will you torment me and crush me with your words?” Words, friend. Words can get heavy. I think a long speech can weigh more than a full bag of flour.

Nobody is staring a hole in Job in this verse. He says they torment him and crush him with their words. Bildad the Shuhite, one of Job's friends, gave a whole speech before this (Job 18). That is a lot of talking, and not a single stare is mentioned.

Job says, “…it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me.” Bildad, Job's friend, had talked about a net catching the wicked (Job 18:8). Here Job says God drew a net around him. Notice he says it straight to his friends, and he doesn't hold back.
Job says, “He has blocked my way so I cannot pass…” A road that just stops is a hard thing to face. And he adds that God has veiled his paths with darkness. That's a blocked way and veiled paths.
Job says, “His troops advance together; they construct a ramp against me and encamp around my tent.” That's the picture he paints. I bet Job felt like it was a lot of army for one man.
A tower makes sense for an army, but Job says ramp. His troops construct a ramp against him and camp around his tent. That's a lot of army for one man. I think that's exactly how Job felt.
A gate isn't in this verse. Job says the troops construct a ramp against him and encamp around his tent. The word he uses is ramp. Just a ramp and a lot of soldiers.
Job says the opposite: “My kinsmen have failed me, and my friends have forgotten me.” That's not standing by him. I think that's a lonely place to be.
Right. Job says his kinsmen have failed him and his friends have forgotten him. That's not standing by him. Kinsmen and friends both, and I think that stings twice.

Job doesn't say they see him as a prophet. He says his guests and maidservants count him as a stranger, and a foreigner in their sight. They count him as someone who doesn't belong. I think that's the sting of it.
Job says, “I call for my servant, but he does not answer, though I implore him with my own mouth.” Job doesn't just call. He implores. I think that part hurts most.
Job says, “Even little boys scorn me; when I appear, they deride me.” That word “even” stands out to me. I think it stings.
The city elders aren't named in this verse. Job says even little boys scorn him, and when he appears they deride him. It's the little boys.
Job says, “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity…” He says it twice. He doesn't ask them to fix anything. I think he just wants them to be gentle.
Advice isn't what Job asks for. He says, “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity…” Pity, twice. I think he wanted a soft landing more than another opinion.
Job wishes his words were written with an iron stylus on lead, “…or chiseled in stone forever.” Whatever he has to say, he wants it to stay. Words in stone don't wash away.

Job says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.” He talks about his skin being destroyed and keeps going. Then comes the “yet.” After that, he says, he will see God in his flesh.

Wealth isn't what Job is talking about here. The verse says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.” The skin is what's named, and the one he says he will see is God. Nothing in this verse is about money.

Job tells his friends, “…then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment.” He's warning them. I think those are heavy words to say to friends.
